issues.issue: The provision both says the Policy 'will lapse' when the Surrender Value on a Monthly Due Date is insufficient and allows a 60 day Grace Period during which the Policy 'continues in full force', so the date lapse actually takes effect is genuinely uncertain. Nothing fixes when the Grace Period begins.

The lapse trigger stated here (insufficient Surrender Value on a Monthly Due Date) must be reconciled with Section 9.4, which lapses the Policy 'whenever' Cash Value less Policy Indebtedness is insufficient and mentions no grace period, and with the first-two-years no-lapse sentence of Section 5.10.
Notice is required 'at least 50 days before the end of the Grace Period' although the Grace Period is only 60 days, leaving a ten-day window whose starting point the Policy never fixes.

The notice duty here overlaps with, and is stated differently from, the special lapse notification required by Section 7.4(10), and its timing depends on the Grace Period commencement left undefined by Section 5.10.
'Adequate premium' is not defined or tied to any stated amount, so what payment averts termination at the end of the Grace Period is left to argument.
Termination 'without value' cannot easily be squared with Section 3.4, which reinstates using the Policy Account Value and Surrender Charges in effect when the Policy lapsed.

Deducting unpaid premium from the Proceeds on a death during the Grace Period presupposes the Policy remains in force, which pulls against Section 5.10's opening statement that the Policy 'will lapse' when the Surrender Value is insufficient on a Monthly Due Date.

The no-lapse test compares cumulative premiums less withdrawals and indebtedness to one-twelfth of the Planned Periodic Premium times months since the Policy Date, but does not say what happens if the test is failed and then later met.
This absolute two-year no-lapse guarantee runs against the general lapse trigger in the first paragraph of Section 5.10 and against the lapse rule in Section 9.4, neither of which carves it out.
Both requirements turn on what is 'satisfactory to us', a standard the Policy nowhere constrains.

The provision states only that Coverage Option A 'may be changed to' Option B on evidence of insurability, leaving it open by negative implication whether a change from Option B to Option A is permitted at all.

The list 'This Policy the application and any supplemental applications' omits punctuation, and the clause does not say whether documents such as the Temporary Insurance Agreement referred to in Section 7.2 or riders form part of the entire contract.
Section 7.2 contemplates a Temporary Insurance Agreement and Sections 2.7 and 5.5 contemplate riders, none of which is named in this integration clause.
The clause makes its limitation of liability 'subject to Section 7.7 - Incontestability', but Incontestability is Section 7.8; Section 7.7 is the age and sex adjustment provision.
Limiting liability to a return of premium where the Insured's health has not 'remained as stated in the application' is in tension with Section 7.8's two-year bar on contesting the Policy.

The sentence is ungrammatical - the Surrender Value 'together with interest ..., deductions for the Monthly Insurance Charges ..., will cause the Policy to lapse' - with no operator joining the credits and the deductions, so the trigger for the special lapse notification cannot be applied as written.
This lapse-warning duty overlaps with, but is stated on a different footing from, the Grace Period notice required by Section 5.10(1).
The two-year suicide period runs 'from the Issue Date', a term Section 2 never defines even though it separately defines Policy Date and Effective Date.
'Issue Date' appears here and in Section 7.8 but nowhere in the Section 2 definitions, which fix instead the Policy Date (2.6) and Effective Date (2.7).

The age and sex misstatement adjustment is stated only in fragments - the benefit is to be 'based on' what the premium 'would have provided, at the correct age and sex' - without a complete operative formula.

The incontestability promise is qualified by the exception 'unless the Surrender Value is insufficient to cover the next Monthly Cost of Insurance', which could be read either as a mere confirmation that the Policy may still lapse or as reopening the insurer's right to contest the Policy entirely.

Section 7.2 makes its return-of-premium remedy 'subject to Section 7.7 - Incontestability', a cross-reference that does not match this section's number and leaves the interaction of the two remedies unsettled.

Conditioning the exercise of 'every right' on there being no assignment cannot be squared with Section 8.3, which contemplates that the Owner's rights merely become 'subject to' an assignment, nor with Section 8.4's change-of-beneficiary machinery.

The change is 'effective upon the date your request was signed' yet has no effect on action taken before the insurer receives it, leaving the status of a signed but undelivered change - and what counts as a form 'satisfactory to us' - open.
The loan-availability clause never states the base from which the deductions are taken, so the maximum loan cannot be computed from the words used.
Deduction 'from the Policy Proceeds' uses a term not defined in Section 2, which defines 'Proceeds'; Section 4.2 states the same deduction as a reduction of the death benefit.

This says the Policy lapses 'whenever' Cash Value less Policy Indebtedness is insufficient for the next Monthly Insurance Charges, with no grace period, while Section 5.10 conditions lapse on the Surrender Value at a Monthly Due Date and allows a 60 day Grace Period.
The option offers payments 'either for a specified period or for a specified amount' but then describes a single present-value computation, without saying which variable is solved for in each branch.

Determining amounts using 'our rates in effect at the time of settlement' omits the guaranteed-rate floors expressly promised in Options 2, 3, 4 and 5 ('never less than 4%' / 'never less than the guaranteed rates'), leaving the two provisions to be harmonised.
The guaranteed periods are listed as 'not less than 5, 10, 15, or 20 years, as elected', but the accompanying table's column headings do not match the periods recited in the text.
